VI. 
Federal and State Income Taxes
9 
Q.
Has the Company made any corrections or updates to federal and state 
10 
income tax expense? 
11 
A.
Yes, the Company made adjustments to reflect changes to the amortization of 
12 
excess accumulated deferred income tax (“ADIT”) and to reflect the flow 
13 
through effect of changes in rate base on income tax expense. 
14 
15 
Q.
Please describe the changes to the amortization of excess ADIT. 
16 
A.
There are two changes effecting the amortization of excess ADIT.  First, the 
17 
overall excess ADIT amount was rolled forward from December 2018 to 
18 
March 2019.  Second the Company changed the amortization life for the 
19 
unprotected, non-plant excess ADIT. 
20 
21 
2224


--- Page 428 ---
Corrections and Updates Testimony of The Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 17 of 24 
Q.
Please explain why the Company rolled forward the excess ADIT 
1 
balances to March 2019. 
2 
A.
The Company rolled the excess ADIT balances forward to match the plant roll 
3 
forward balance and to reflect adjustments to income tax reserves that resulted 
4 
from the settlement of the August 24, 2007 to March 31, 2009 federal income 
5 
tax audit.  For the audit adjustments that were temporary, the current income 
6 
tax was booked at 35 percent, the deferred tax was booked at 21 percent, and 
7 
the difference increased or decreased the regulatory liability for excess ADIT. 
8 
The amortization lives were applied to the adjusted balances, resulting in 
9 
changed total excess ADIT amortization amounts. 
10 
11 
Q.
Were there any other changes related to the amortization of excess 
12 
ADIT? 
13 
A.
Yes, the Company made adjustments to the amortization period for excess 
14 
ADIT and to reflect shifts between unprotected and protected excess ADIT. 
15 
As KEDLI was an asset purchase, there was a tax basis adjustment in the 
16 
PowerTax system that represented the book depreciation reserve at the time of 
17 
the asset purchase.  Originally, during the implementation of the module, no 
18 
book depreciation was allocated to this purchase accounting adjustment when 
19 
it should have attracted book depreciation.  The allocation of book 
20 
depreciation was corrected in a later version.  This resulted in the protected 
21 
2225


--- Page 429 ---
Corrections and Updates Testimony of The Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 18 of 24 
excess ADIT decreasing and the unprotected plant excess ADIT increasing. 
1 
This also resulted in lower annual protected amortization amounts.  These 
2 
adjusted amounts are set forth in Exhibit ___ (RRP-6CU), Workpaper 1 in a 
3 
manner similar to the April 30 filing.  However, using the remaining book life 
4 
of 47 years for unprotected plant amortization life and 14 years for 
5 
unprotected non-plant balances resulted in an annual recovery from customers 
6 
rather than a return of excess ADIT, as would be expected.  To avoid 
7 
collecting from customers only to return the money in a future period, the 
8 
Company proposes to increase the recovery period of unprotected non-plant 
9 
excess ADIT to 25 years to reverse the negative impact. 
10

Deferred Taxes
1 
Q.

2

3 
A.
The Company made changes to rate base ADIT to (i) flow through the impact 
4

5 
on the fiscal year end March 31, 2019 federal income tax return, (iii) update 
6

7

8

9 
10 
Q.
How does the change in excess ADIT amortization change rate base? 
11 
A.
As the Company returns excess ADIT, excess ADIT regulatory liability that is 
12 
included in rate base decreases and rate base is correspondingly increased. 
13 
Rate base ADIT adjustments were made to reflect the updated amortization 
14 
amounts that flow through cost of service.  Also, the Company determined 
15 
that in the April 30 filing, the rate base adjustment included the excess ADIT 
16 
related to both National Grid USA Service Company and KEDLI. 
17 
Accordingly, the Company updated the rate base formula to include only the 
18 
amortization related to KEDLI. 
19 
20 
21 
2228


--- Page 432 ---
Corrections and Updates Testimony of The Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 21 of 24 
Q.
How did bonus depreciation change rate base ADIT?  
1 
A.
After additional analysis and conversations with industry experts and other 
2 
industry peers, the Company determined it would deduct additional bonus 
3 
depreciation, in accordance with the pre-tax reform regulations.  Bonus 
4 
depreciation will be 40 percent for those assets started before September 28, 
5 
2017 and placed in service between April 1, 2018 and December 31, 2018. 
6 
Bonus depreciation of 30 percent will be taken on assets started before 
7 
September 28, 2017 and placed in service between January 1 and March 31, 
8 
2019.  As the consolidated National Grid group is in a net operating loss 
9 
(“NOL”) utilization position for the fiscal year, additional bonus depreciation 
10 
deductions will result in a reduction of the NOL utilization that is also 
11 
reflected in KEDLI’s rate base changes.

J.
Savings
12 
Q.
What level of savings is typically reflected in a rate filing? 
13 
A.
Rate cases traditionally include a productivity adjustment on the premise 
14 
that well-run companies should be able to find a modest measure of 
15 
efficiencies in the rate year.  The adjustment is typically calculated as one 
16 
percent of total labor expense and payroll taxes in recognition of how 
17 
difficult it is to achieve savings year after year.  In this case, the traditional 
18 
productivity adjustment would result in efficiencies totaling $2.020 
19 
million.  The Company, however, has proposed to provide customers with 
20 
more than $15 million in savings in the Rate Year – a level more than 
21 
2264


--- Page 468 ---
Case 19-G-0310 
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 31 of 51 
seven times the traditional productivity adjustment.  The SRRP asserts that 
1 
$3.220 million of additional efficiencies should be imputed above this 
2 
level.  If the SRRP’s position were adopted, this would equate to savings 
3 
of more than nine times the traditional productivity adjustment, which is 
4 
simply unrealistic and not supported.   
5 
6 
Q.
Will the level of savings reflected by the Company in the rate filing be 
7 
difficult to achieve? 
8 
A.
Yes.  It is a challenge for any business to achieve a one percent efficiency 
9 
reduction each year let alone seven times that number.  In its filing, the 
10 
Company committed to reduce its costs through an ambitious effort (the 
11 
Accelerate Program), despite that many of the initiatives to achieve these 
12 
reductions are difficult and potentially not sustainable.  Indeed, the 
13 
Company is working tirelessly to reduce its costs to mitigate bill impacts 
14 
for customers while continuing to invest to assure reliability and advance 
15 
our systems for the future.   
16 
17 
To reduce costs to the magnitude the Company proposes in this filing 
18 
requires major changes to people, processes, and systems.  This requires 
19 
time and effort.  There is a major risk that the savings will not be realized 
20 
because competing priorities will distract from the Company’s ability to 
21 
2265


--- Page 469 ---
Case 19-G-0310 
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 32 of 51 
deliver the initiatives.  For example, new work, changes in law, new 
1 
regulatory requirements, changes in customer expectations, or major 
2 
weather events could all impact the Company’s ability to progress 
3 
initiatives or deliver savings.  Staff’s filing further exacerbates this risk 
4 
through their proposals to disallow costs that the Company will need to 
5 
incur in the Rate Year to ensure the delivery of safe and reliable service.   
6 
7 
Q.
The SRRP asserts that savings associated with Implementation Level 
8 
(“IL”) 3 Accelerate Program initiatives should be imputed into the 
9 
revenue requirement, contending that savings from these initiatives 
10 
“have been identified and quantified,” and been defined by the 
11 
Company as “bankable” (at 56-57).  Does the Panel agree? 
12 
A.
No.  While IL3 Accelerate Program initiatives have been assigned an 
13 
initial estimate of potential savings, the estimate is aspirational as the 
14 
business has not taken any of the steps that are necessary to implement the 
15 
initiative.  In IL3, the business develops a plan to implement an initiative. 
16 
Until each step in the implementation plan has been completed, whether 
17 
the initiative can be delivered and the savings ultimately achieved is 
18 
unknown.  As the Company explained in the response to IR DPS-755, 
19 
“bankable” means that the Company is willing to invest the time and 
20 
resources into pursuing the initiative, as the Company has limited 
21 
2266


--- Page 470 ---
Case 19-G-0310 
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 33 of 51 
resources to dedicate to implementing initiatives.  This does not mean that 
1 
the initiative can actually deliver savings, however.  There are risks that 
2 
this initial estimate, which is really a placeholder to prioritize initiatives, 
3 
may never materialize or may change materially.  These risks include 
4 
changes in assumptions as the initiative progresses, delays in 
5 
implementation, or cancelation of the initiative because, despite the 
6 
Company’s efforts, the implementation plan could not be delivered (e.g., a

9 
SRRP’s position, IL3 estimates are not quantified let alone known and

measurable, which is the standard for inclusion in the revenue

12 
efficiency initiatives that are properly subsumed within the traditional

In the Panel’s direct testimony, we explained the rigorous process

undertaken to progress initiatives.  Each initiative must pass through

implementation levels ranging from IL0 (purely an idea) to IL5 (fully 
18 
implemented), where they are scrutinized by groups from the Company’s

not until IL4 where an initiative undergoes implementation.  In IL4 the 
21 
2267


--- Page 471 ---

business has completed the steps in its implementation plan that are a

C.
Earnings Sharing Mechanism
8 
9 
Q.
The Staff Policy Panel (“SPP”) recommends (at 12-14) that the 
10 
Commission establish an Earnings Sharing Mechanism (“ESM”) for 
11 
the Companies for each 12-month period following the Rate Year. 
12 
Does the Panel agree with this recommendation? 
13 
A.
No, we do not.  ESMs are typically a feature of multi-year rate plans that 
14 
are submitted to the Commission as joint proposals that reflect the broad 
15 
agreement of most, if not all, parties to Commission rate proceedings.  It is 
16 
our understanding that the Commission only recently imposed an ESM in 
17 
a litigated one-year rate proceeding.  From our perspective, imposing 
18 
ESMs in litigated cases would be poor regulatory policy in that it would 
19 
discourage the Companies from finding ways to manage their businesses 
20 
in a manner that minimizes the need for time consuming and expensive 
21 
rate proceedings.  Moreover, the SPP’s ESM recommendation essentially 
22 
2280


--- Page 484 ---
Case 19-G-0310 
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 47 of 51 
requests the Commission to impose a mechanism that would confiscate a 
1 
portion of the Companies’ earnings without making a finding as to what a 
2 
just and reasonable ROE would be in years beyond the Rate Year or 
3 
conducting the process that is typically followed in establishing utility 
4 
rates. 
5 
6 
Q. 
Please explain. 
7 
A.
In this case, the Commission is setting rates that it will determine to be 
8 
just and reasonable for a Rate Year beginning April 1, 2020 and ending 
9 
March 31, 2021.  Among the decisions being made is the appropriate ROE 
10 
that should be applied to the Company’s rate base during this period.  As 
11 
the Commission is aware, the just and reasonable ROE changes over time. 
12 
However, if this case is litigated, the Commission will make no finding as 
13 
to what the appropriate ROE for the Company will be for any period 
14 
beyond the Rate Year.  At the same time, however, under the SPP’s ESM 
15 
mechanism in years beyond the Rate Year, the Company could be required 
16 
to forfeit a portion of its earnings regardless of whether those earnings 
17 
would, depending on capital market conditions at the time, be no greater 
18 
than the amount needed to enable the Company to earn a compensatory 
19 
ROE.  Such a result would be procedurally defective and substantively 
20 
confiscatory. 
21 
2281


--- Page 485 ---
Case 19-G-0310 
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 48 of 51 
1 
The Commission has the ability under the Public Service Law to monitor 
2 
the Company’s earnings and take appropriate action to the extent that it 
3 
believes that the Company’s rates are producing excessive returns.  There 
4 
is no need for the Commission to impose an ESM to ensure that rates 
5 
remain just and reasonable and it is quite possible that the results of 
6 
imposing such a mechanism would not be just and reasonable.  For these 
7 
reasons, the SPP’s ESM recommendation should be rejected.

III. 
Updates to the Revenue Requirement
14 
Q.
Please explain the impact of the NE:NY Order on the Company’s 
15 
revenue requirement. 
16 
A.
As supported by the Future of Heat Panel, the Company used the energy 
17 
efficiency targets and budgets set forth in the Commission’s December 13, 
18 
2018 “Order Adopting Accelerated Energy Efficiency Targets” in Case 18-
19 
M-0084 (“Accelerated Efficiency Order”) to set the proposed Rate Year
20 
energy efficiency rate allowance of $9.478 million.  This amount was 
21 
exclusive of $0.171 million of pass through Clean Energy Fund expenses 
22 
and $0.474 million of evaluation, measurement, and verification 
23 
2300


--- Page 504 ---
Page 3 of 7 
(“EM&V”) costs that the Company originally proposed to move to base 
1 
rates and track outside of the energy efficiency portfolio.  Additionally, the 
2 
Company proposed to include the costs of its low-income energy efficiency 
3 
HEAT Program ($2.5 million) in base rates.   
4 
5 
The NE:NY Order increased KEDLI’s energy efficiency budget by an 
6 
incremental $1.232 million in the Rate Year, as compared to the budget 
7 
established in the Accelerated Efficiency Order.  In addition, the NE:NY 
8 
Order provided that EM&V costs are included in the authorized energy 
9 
efficiency budgets established by the Commission.  Based on the foregoing, 
10 
KEDLI is adjusting its revenue requirement to incorporate the incremental 
11 
energy efficiency budget increase, remove EM&V costs from base rates, 
12 
and remove the costs of the HEAT Program, as the HEAT program costs 
13 
will be funded through the increase to the energy efficiency budget.  Table 
14 
1 on page 5 summarizes the changes to the revenue requirement.   
15 
16 
Q.
Is the Company proposing any additional updates to the revenue 
17 
requirement to address the impacts of the NE:NY Order? 
18 
A.
Yes.  As explained by the Future of Heat Panel, to meet the new targets set 
19 
forth in the NE:NY Order, address the compliance and reporting 
20 
requirements, and to help optimize the energy efficiency portfolio to 
21 
2301


--- Page 505 ---
Page 4 of 7 
achieve maximum customer benefits, the Company updated the revenue 
1 
requirement to reflect KEDLI’s allocable share of eight incremental FTEs. 
2 
KEDLI proposes to phase in the FTEs throughout the Rate Year and Data 
3 
Year 1 as it implements the provisions of the EE Order.  The request 
4 
increases the revenue requirement by $0.258 million in the Rate Year. 
5 
6 
Q.
Does the Panel have any additional comments about the NE:NY Order? 
7 
A.
Yes.  The Company recognizes the Commission’s expectation in the 
8 
NE:NY Order that any uncommitted and unspent energy efficiency funds 
9 
be applied to mitigate the cost of expanded energy efficiency programs. 
10 
While KEDLI generally supports the use of regulatory liabilities to mitigate 
11 
customer bills, the Company has concern for using significant regulatory 
12 
liabilities to offset the revenue requirement in this case without considering 
13 
the cash flow implications, the Company’s regulatory asset position, and 
14 
the long-term ratemaking implication.  Indeed, KEDLI has a significant 
15 
regulatory asset balance on its books that the Company is not proposing to 
16 
recover from customers in this rate filing - but must be addressed eventually. 
17 
Therefore, the Company believes there must be a balance between the 
18 
appropriate level of regulatory liabilities used now and those reserved for 
19 
future rate mitigation. 
20 
21

13 
Earnings Base Capitalization/Working Capital 
14 
Q.
Have the Companies made adjustments to the 
15 
Earnings Base Capitalization (EB/CAP) adjustment 
16 
and working capital components in rate base in 
17 
projecting the Rate Year? 
18 
A.
Yes.  While both KEDNY and KEDLI make EB/CAP and 
19 
working capital adjustments, our recommended 
20 
adjustments relate solely to KEDNY. 
21 
Q.
Please explain the Earnings Base Capitalization 
22 
(EB/CAP) adjustment that is reflected in rate 
23 
base. 
24 
2400


--- Page 604 ---
Cases 19-G-0309 & 19-G-0310 
SRRP 
69
A.
The EB/CAP adjustment aligns the utility rate 
1 
base with its capitalization devoted to utility 
2 
service.  Utilities are allowed a return only on 
3 
the capital devoted to utility service so that 
4 
customers pay no more, and utilities recover no 
5 
less, than the indicated return on the capital 
6 
supporting utility operations. 
7 
Q.
What is the capitalization used in the EB/CAP? 
8 
A.
Capitalization for the EB/CAP represents funds 
9 
provided by investors and customers supporting 
10 
utility operations, on which utilities pay a 
11 
return.  Some examples of capitalization, as 
12 
used here, include: common stock, retained 
13 
earnings, advances from associated companies, 
14 
and short-term debt.  Accordingly, these items 
15 
create a cost that must be recovered through 
16 
utility rates.  In addition, as capitalization 
17 
supports all assets, it must be reduced for 
18 
assets that are not part of utility operations.  
19 
Assets that are not part of utility operations, 
20 
for which capitalization must be reduced, 
21 
include assets such as temporary cash 
22 
investments, non-utility property, internal 
23 
reserves, and goodwill.  In other words, for 
24 
2401


--- Page 605 ---
Cases 19-G-0309 & 19-G-0310 
SRRP 
70
purposes of the EB/CAP adjustment, 
1 
capitalization could include more items than the 
2 
term would usually imply when used generally to 
3 
describe the utility’s capital structure. 
4 
Q.
Generally, why does a utility’s rate base not 
5 
equal its capitalization? 
6 
A.
The causes of the EB/CAP differential vary at 
7 
each utility but are generally variations in 
8 
cash flow items not in rate base, such as non-
9 
interest bearing liabilities, or cost-free 
10 
sources of funds, that support a utility’s 
11 
assets resulting from the timing of payments on 
12 
accounts payable, sales, and other taxes 
13 
payable.  Another cause of the EB/CAP 
14 
differential may be imperfections in the 
15 
estimation of cash working capital funding 
16 
requirements. 
17 
Q.
Is a utility’s rate base supported entirely by 
18 
cost-bearing capital, such as: common capital 
19 
stock, preferred Stock, retained earnings, long-
20 
term debt, and short-term debt? 
21 
A.
No.  Utilities have access to cost-free sources 
22 
of funds, due to the delay of when the amount is 
23 
recovered from customers, and the actual payment 
24 
2402


--- Page 606 ---
Cases 19-G-0309 & 19-G-0310 
SRRP 
71
is made.  Specifically, this results with 
1 
accounts such as taxes payable, and accounts 
2 
payable.  However, utilities do not pay a 
3 
return, and have no capital cost associated 
4 
with, accounts or taxes payable.  Also, 
5 
utilities provide cost free capital or use of 
6 
funds to customers.  For example, utilities do 
7 
not receive a return on current customer 
8 
accounts receivable for utility service.  The 
9 
net amount of these short-term cost-free capital 
10 
requirements is usually referred to as working 
11 
capital, which is included in the utility’s rate 
12 
base. 
13 
Q.
What is KEDNY’s Rate Year forecast of the EB/CAP 
14 
adjustment? 
15 
A.
As shown on Exhibit___(RRP-7CU), Summary, KEDNY 
16 
computed a Historic Test Year EB/CAP adjustment

18

20 
$90.609 million to project a Rate Year EB/CAP

22 
million.  In addition to the normalizing 
23 
adjustments to EB/CAP, KEDNY made offsetting 
24 
2403


--- Page 607 ---
Cases 19-G-0309 & 19-G-0310 
SRRP 
72

1 
identified working capital component of rate

19

as a simpler, but reasonably accurate, gauge of

required working capital.

Staff Review 
1 
Q.
Please provide a brief description of the 
2 
Companies’ historical property tax expense. 
3 
A.
KEDNY and KEDLI’s historical property tax 
4 
expense includes property taxes paid to New York 
5 
City and paid to taxing authorities outside New 
6 
York City, i.e., to counties, cities, towns, 
7 
villages, and schools on Long Island.  KEDNY 
8

9 
pays taxes to both New York City and taxing 
10

11 
Q.
How does New York City tax property? 
12 
A.
New York City, taxes property in four tax 
13 
categories or classes, Class 1 and 2 are forms 
14 
of residential property, while Class 3 includes 
15 
all special franchise real utility property, 
16 
with the exception of land and buildings.  Class 
17

Economic and Functional Obsolescence 
13 
Q.
Please describe Economic Obsolescence (EO). 
14 
A.
EO is the “loss of value of property caused by 
15 
an impairment in desirability or useful life 
16 
resulting from factors external to the 
17 
property,” as defined in Title 20 of the New 
18 
York Code of Rules and Regulations, Part 8197-
19 
2.8(b). 
20 
Q.
Please explain the EO process and how it affects 
21 
property tax expense. 
22 
A.
Utilities apply for an EO allowance by 
23 
submitting a standard calculation to ORPTS.  The 
24 
2576


--- Page 780 ---
Cases 19-G-0309 & 19-G-0310  SAP SECOND CORRECTED 
32
calculation compares a five-year average of 
1 
actual return on rate base to the allowed return 
2 
on rate base.  ORPTS then reviews the 
3 
calculations and makes a formal determination on 
4 
the EO awarded to utilities.  The EO allowance 
5 
is applied as a percentage reduction to a 
6 
utility’s assessed special franchise property, 
7 
which effectively reduces property tax expense. 
8 
Q.
Please describe Functional Obsolescence (FO). 
9 
A.
FO is “the impairment of operating capacity or 
10 
efficiency resulting in a loss in value brought 
11 
about by the failure of the tangible property to 
12 
meet present or projected needs or where the 
13 
capacity of the tangible property exceeds 
14 
reasonable anticipated demands,” as defined in 
15 
Title 20 of the New York Code of Rules and 
16 
Regulations, Part 8197-2.8(c).  An FO allowance 
17 
also applies a percentage that reduces 
18 
assessable values for special franchise 
19 
property, thus reducing property tax expense. 
20 
Q.
Is there a standard for how FO is calculated? 
21 
A.
No.  There is no specific standard for how to 
22 
calculate an FO allowance.  The utility would 
23 
have to make a filing to ORPTS to demonstrate 
24 
2577


--- Page 781 ---
Cases 19-G-0309 & 19-G-0310  SAP SECOND CORRECTED 
33
that a loss in value occurred. 
1 
Q.

2 
Year expenses net of EO and FO? 
3 
A.
Yes.  KEDNY and KEDLI reflected EO and FO 
4 
percentage reductions embedded in the actual 
5 
property tax expenses for the Historic Test 
6 
Year.
